newsitem.title: UK: Europe chemical costs little changed despite EU.
newsitem.headline: Europe chemical costs little changed despite EU.

text.p: The European single market has had little overall impact on costs in the European Union's chemical industry, according to a survey by consultants KPMG presented on Wednesday.

KPMG partner Michael Littlechild told the annual business outlook conference of Britain's Chemical Industries Assocation that efforts to facilitate trade between EU countries had improved competitiveness and cut some costs, but benefits had been largely offset by increasing environmental legislation.
More than half of companies surveyed believed the internal market had raised their costs because of EU rules on packaging and labelling.
But this was offset by falls in transport costs as internal border controls were simplified and by lower capital and finance costs.
"On balance costs seem unchanged," Littlechild said.
The full details of the KPMG survey of the industry, which was carried out on behalf of the European Commission, are to be publis shortly.

The survey, based on 60 in-depth interviews with chemical companies across the EU supplemented by a postal survey, compared the period between 1980 and 1987 with the five-years from 1988 to 1992, when much of the legislation enacting a single European market was put in place.
The single market, which was aimed at abolishing trade barriers for business across the EU, was given a starting date of 1992 by the European Commission, although it is still not complete.
KPMG found that the total level of exports from one EU country to another rose in the five years to 1992, but found no evidence of a "Fortress Europe," with non-EU imports also rising.

Littlechild said the survey also found that the "percentage of companies that exported (to other EU states) jumped quite significantly, which adds weight to the hypothesis that they were able to do so more easily."

Some 80 percent of chemical companies said they faced greater competition from other EU states, compared with around 15 percent citing North America and just over 10 percent Eastern European countries.

Encouragingly for the European Commission 55 percent of companies intervied face-to-face said price differentials between EU states had narrowed, with nearly 40 percent attributing the drop to the single market. KPMG said that agrochemicals, dyes and pigments and inorganic chemicals had seen costs drop to the greatest extent as a result of increased competition.

Nearly 70 percentof companies said they had seen efficiency gains through higher investment in response to the challenge of greater competition, and a similar proportion said they had cut their workforce as a result. More than 60 percent said there had been little impact on profit margins from the single market.
Littlechild also cited a Department of Trade and industry survey which ofund that 81 percent of British chemical companies "encountered no difficulty in exporting to the EU."
